Atlus Space Builders Ms. Anjali, Advocate
Pvt. Ltd. Ms. Latika Vashisht, Advocate

For the Respondents Mr. Ramhik Gupta, Advocate
(in FA/42/2022)
For other Respondents : NEMO

 ORDER
PER BHARATKUMAR PANDYA. MEMBER
1. These are the appeals arising out of the common order dated 29.11.2021
passed in CC/16, 97 and 122 of 2020 passed by the Chandigarh State Commission.
The complaint involved a builder-buyer dispute. The complaints have been allowed
and as mentioned in detail in the impugned order, the refunds of the consideration
amounts paid by the complainants have been allowed with further direction for
payment of compensatory interest thereon at 12%, (15% in case payment not made
within 30 days) for the period from the respective date of deposits till the date of
payment. The operative portion of the order dated 29.11.2021 passed by the State
Commission is reproduced below:
"20. Since, it is an admitted fact that possession of respective plots has not been offered
 till the date of filing of these consumer complaints or thereafter, as such, there is a
 continuing cause of action in favour of the complainants to file these complaints in view of
 law laid down in
Lata Construction & Ors. Vs. Dr. Rameshchandra Ramniklal Shah and
 Ann, II
2000 (1}
CPC
269-AIR 1999 SC 380 and Meerut Development Authority Vs.
 Mukesh Kumar Gupta. IV (2012) CPJ 12 ISC), wherein it was held that when actual
 physical possession of the residential units is not delivered, there is a continuing cause of
 action in favour of the allottee/buyer. Objection raised in this regard, as such, stands
 rejected.
21. Now coming to the objection taken to the effect that opposite party no.4/The Greater
 Punjab Officer's Co-operative House Building Society is not a necessary party to this
 complaint, against which also, the complainants have sought refund of the amount paid.
 It may be stated here that it has been fairly admitted by opposite parties no. 1 to 3 in their
joint written statement filed in CC No. 16 Of 2020 and also during arguments by their
 Counsel that the amounts
,
referred to above
, in the respective complaints, have been
 received by them (opposite parties no. 1 to 3). Furthermore, during argument also, it has
 also been fairly admitted by Counsel for opposite parties no. 1 to 3 that they (opposite
parties no. 1 to 3) were liable to offer and deliver possession of the respective plots to the
 complainants in the above said complaints. In this view of the matter, it is held that
 complaints against the Greater Punjab Officer's Co-operative House Building Society
 deserve to be dismissed.
22. As far as contention raised by Counsel for opposite parties no. 1
to 3, who also appeared on behalf of opposite party no. 4 (yet it was debarred for filing
reply/evidence vide order dated 23.11.2020) to the effect that the company is answerable
for the amounts against which payment receipts have from the complainants, in each
case, against which receipts have been issued been issued, it may be stated here that
over and above the amount received by them (opposite parties no. 1 to 31. the rest of the
amount/s) received in cash have also been acknowledged by opposite party no.5/M/s
Ajeet Associates, as under:-
i) In CC No. 16 of 2020 = Receipt of Rs. 7 lacs in cash has been acknowledged by
 M/s Ajeet Associates vide agreement to sell dated 15.06.2011, Annexure C-8.
ii) In CC No.97 of 2020 Receipt of Rs.2 lacs and Rs.2,56,250/-in cash has been
 acknowledged by M/s Ajeet Associates vide agreement to sell dated 10.11.2010,
 Annexure C-8.
Hi) In CC No. 121 of 2020 = Receipt of Rs.7,50,000/- and Rs.5 lara in cash has
 been acknowledged by M/s Ajeet Associates vide agreement to sell dated
 14.10.2011, Annexure C-11.
In this view of the matter, it is held that the objection taken by opposite parties no. 1 to 3
and also on behalf of opposite party no. 4, through their Counsel, to the effect that they are
not answerable for any amount paid in cash by the complainants, in each case, being
devoid of merit, stands rejected.
23. Counsel for the complainants, while placing reliance on
New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
Vs. HUH Multipurpose Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd.. Civil Appeal
no. 10941-10942 of 2013.
decided by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India on 04.03.2020. contended with
vehemence that since there has been delay on the part of opposite parties no. 1 to 3 in
filing reply and evidence, beyond 45 days, as such, their application bearing no.251 of
2020 seeking extension of time for filing the same be dismissed.
It may be stated here that
we have gone through the contents of the
New India Assurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Hilli
Multipurpose Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd.
's case (supra) and find that though it has been held
by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that the District Forum has no power to extend the
time for filing reply to the complaint beyond the total period of 45 days, yet, it has also
been held that
the said judgment
will be operated prospectively i.e. after 04.03.2020.
However, the present complaint had been filed by the complainant on 13.01.2020 i.e.
before 04.03.2020 when the order aforesaid was passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of
India and it was only on 22.01.2020, that the opposite parties were ordered to file reply
and evidence by way of affidavit.
Thus, keeping in mind the fact that the principle of law
laid down by
the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India vide order dated 04.03.2020 passed in
New India Assurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd.
's case (sunral
was to be operated prospectively, whereas, on the other hand, the present case had been
filed on 13.01.2020, as such, the application bearing no.251 of 2020 stood allowed with no
order as to cost.
24. For the reasons recorded above, all the three complaints are partly accepted, with
costs as under:-
In CC No.16 of 2020, opposite parties no.1 to 3 and 5, jointly and severally, are
directed to:-
i) Refund the amount of Rs.56,62,500/- to the complainant, alongwith compensation
 by way of interest @12%> p.a., without deducting any TDS, from the respective dates
 of deposit onwards, within a period of 30 days, from the date of receipt of a certified
 copy of this order, failing which, thereafter, the said amount shall carry 3% penal
 interest i.e. 15%> p.a. (12% p.a. plus (+) 3% p.a.), from the date of passing of this
 order, till realization.
ii) Pay compensation for causing mental agony and physical harassment;
deficiency in providing service and adoption of unfair trade practice and also
 cost of litigation, in lumpsum, to the tune of Rs.1,35,000/- to the complainant
 within a period of 30 days from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this
 order, failing which, the said amount shall carry interest @9% p.a. from the date
 of passing of this order, till realization.
Hi) Complaint against opposite party no.4/The Greater Punjab Officer's
 Co-operative House Building Society is dismissed with no order as to costs.
In CC No.97 of 2020. opposite parties no.1 to 3 and 5. jointly and severally, are
directed to:-
i) Refund the amount of Rs.28,39,830/- to the complainant, alongwith
 compensation by way of interest @12% p.a., without deducting any TDS, from the
 respective dates of deposit onwards, within a period of 30 days, from the date of
 receipt of a certified copy of this order, failing which, thereafter, the said amount
 shall carry 3%> penal interest i.e. 15% p.a. (12% p.a. plus (+) 3%> p.a.), from the
 date of passing of this order, till realization.
ii) Pay compensation for causing mental agony and physical harassment;
deficiency in providing service and adoption of unfair trade practice and also cost of
 litigation, in lumpsum, to the tune of Rs. 1,35,000/- to the complainant within a
 period of 30 days from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this order, failing
 which, the said amount shall carry interest @9% p.a. from the date of passing of
 this order, till realization.
Hi) Complaint against opposite party no.4/The Greater Punjab Officer's
 Co-operative House Building Society is dismissed with no order as to costs.
In CC No.121 of 2020. opposite parties no.1 to 4 and 6, jointly and severally, are
directed to:-
i) Refund the amount of Rs.40,37,180/- to the complainants, alongwith
 compensation by way of interest @12% p.a., without deducting any IDS, from the
 respective dates of deposit onwards, within a period of 30 days, from the date of
 receipt of a certified copy of this order, failing which, thereafter, the said amount
 shall carry 3% penal interest i.e. 15% p.a. (12%> p.a. plus (+) 3%> p.a.), from the
 date of passing of this order, till realization.
ii) Pay compensation for causing mental agony and physical harassment;
deficiency in providing service and adoption of unfair trade practice and also cost of
 litigation, in lumpsum, to the tune of Rs.1,35,000/- to the complainants within a
 period of 30 days from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this order, failing
 which, the said amount shall carry interest @9% p.a. from the date of passing of
 this order, till realization.
Hi) Complaint against opposite party no.5/The Greater Punjab Officer's
 Co-operative House Building Society and opposite party 38 UT Che no.7/M/s
 Reliance Capital Limited & Reliance Property Solutions is dismissed with no order
 as to costs.
25. However, it is made clear that in case the complainants, in any of the complaints
 above, have availed housing loan from any Bank(s)/financial institution(s) for making
 payment towards price of their respective plots, it shall have the first charge of the amount
 payable, to the extent, the same is due to be paid by them, in each case. "
2. As can be seen, the allottees have been granted the refund of the consideration
paid by them with compensatory interest, The present appeal nos. FA/42, 43 and
44/2022 have been filed by the developer. The builder is aggrieved not by the finding
of the deficient service as arrived at by the State Commission but only by the
quantum of compensation granted, i.e. the rate of compensatory interest granted by
the State Commission. The appellant is also aggrieved that the compensations under
multiple heads have been granted by the State Commission which is against the law
as
laid down by
the Supreme Court in the case of D.S. Dhanda. Relying upon the
following decisions, it has been vehemently urged by Mr. Yogesh Dass, learned
counsel for the appellant builder that the rate of interest of 12% (and on default, 15%)
is excessive and unreasonable and is inconsistent with the rate of interest of 9%
allowed by the Apex court in the following decisions, wherefrom, the observations in
few of the decisions are also reproduced below:
1. TDI Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. Vs. Shakti Kumar Jain & Anr, in FA No. 636/2020
 decided on 14.05.2024,
2.
Experion Developers Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Sushma Ashok Shiroor
(2022) SCC Online SC 416,
3.
NBCC (india) Ltd. Vs. Shri Ram Trivedi
(2021) 5 SCC 273,
4.
Ireo Grace Realtech Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Abhishek Khanna & Ors.
(2021) 3 SCC 241,
5.
DLF Home Developers Ltd. & Anr. Vs. Capital Greens Flat Buyers Association & Ors
.
(2021) 5 SCC 537,
6.
Arifur Rehman Khan & Ors. Vs. DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
(2020) 16 SCC 512,
7.
DLF Home Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. Vs. D.S. Dhanda & Ors.
(2020) 16 SCC 318, M/s
Suneja Towers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. Vs. Anita Merchant
in C.A. 2892-2894/2023 arising out of
 SLP (Civil) No. 8163-8165 decided on 18.04.2023, and
8.
MiHi Jain Vs. Wave City Centre Pvt. Ltd.
in CC No. 3304/2017 decided on 29.10.2021.
DLF Homes Panchkula (P) Ltd. v. D.S. Dhanda
, (2020) 16 SCC 318
17. This Court in a judgment reported as
Irrigation Department, State of Orissa v. G.C. Roy
 [Irrigation Department
,
State of Orissa v. G.C. Roy
, (1992) 1 SCC 508] examined the question
 as to whether an arbitrator has the power to award interest pendente lite. It was held that a
 person deprived of use of money to which he is legitimately entitled has a right to be
 compensated for the deprivation which may be called interest, compensation or damages.
 Thus, keeping in view the said principle
laid down in
the aforesaid judgment, the amount of
 the interest is the compensation to the beneficiary deprived of the use of the investment made
 by the complainant. Therefore, such interest will take into its ambit, the consequences of
 delay in not handing over his possession. In fact, we find that the learned Scdrc as well as
 Ncdrc has awarded compensation under different heads on account of singular default of not
 handing over possession. Such award under various heads in respect of the same default is
 not sustainable.
18. Thus, we find that the complainant is entitled to interest from the appellant for not handing
 over possession as projected as is offered by it but it is not a case to award special punitive
 damages as one of the causes for late delivery of possession was beyond the control of the
 appellant. Therefore, in view of the settlement proposal submitted by the appellant in earlier
 two set of appeals in respect of same project, and to settle any further controversy, the
 appellant is directed as follows:
21. We find that the grant of interest @ 15% by Scdrc is highly excessive. Since in other two
 set of appeals decided earlier, this Court has awarded interest @ 9% p.a. on the amount of
 refund, therefore, the order of Scdrc stand modified so as to pay interest @ 9% p.a. from the
 date of deposit till the date of refund.
Experion Developers (P) Ltd. v. Sushma Ashok Shiroor
, (2022) 15 SCC
286
14.
In
Arifur Rahman Khan v. DLF Southern Homes (P) Ltd. [Arifur Rahman Khan
v. DLF
 Southern Homes (P) Ltd., (2020) 16 SCC 512], this Court held that there is no embargo on
 the award of compensation beyond the rate stipulated in the apartment buyer's agreement
 where handing over the possession of the flat has been delayed. The Court observed that the
 Consumer Forums must take a robust and a common-sense approach by taking judicial
 notice of the fact that flat purchasers obtained loans and are required to pay EMIs to financial
 institutions for subserving their debts. The delay compensation clause provided for Rs 5 per
 square foot per month. This Court found that this stipulation is clearly one-sided and does not
 maintain a level platform or even reflect a bargain between the parties. The Court granted
 additional compensation @ 6% p.a. simple interest to each buyer therein, over and above the
 delay compensation clause.
15.
In
NBCC (India) Ltd. v. Ram Trivedi [NBCC (India) Ltd.
v. Ram Trivedi, (2021) 5 SCC 273:
(2021) 3 SCC (Civ) 1], the Court found that the agreement fastening liability on the purchaser
 to pay simple interest @12% p.a. if he failed to pay instalments on time and at the same time,
 if the seller failed to hand over the possession on time, he would have to pay compensation
 only @ of Rs 2 per square feet would constitute an unfair trade practice. The Court held that a
 term of a contract would not be final and binding if it is shown that the flat purchasers have no
 option but to sign on the dotted line of a contract framed by the builders. The
Court further
 held
that Consumer Forums were empowered to award just and reasonable compensation as
 an incident of its power to direct removal of a deficiency in service; they are not constrained
 by the rate prescribed in the agreement. The Court held that the compensation could be
 granted even if possession had been delivered.
The same principle is followed in a
 subsequent decision in
DLF Home Developers Ltd. v. Capital Greens Flat Buyers Assn. [DLF
 Home Developers Ltd.
v. Capital Greens Flat Buyers Assn., (2021) 5 SCC 537: (2021) 3 SCC
 (Civ) 397]
31. On the other hand, the appellant Developer submitted that (i) period for interest should be
 linked to the estimated date of possession and not the date of payments, and (ii) the rate of
 interest must be the rate provided in the
Interest Act, 1978
.
32. We are of the opinion that for the interest payable on the amount deposited to be
 restitutionary and also compensatory, interest has to be paid from the date of the deposit of
 the amounts. The Commission in the order impugned has granted interest from the date of
 last deposit. We find that this does not amount to restitution. Following the decision in DLF
 Homes Panchkula (P) Ltd. v. D.S. Dhanda [DLF Homes Panchkula (P) Ltd. v. D.S. Dhanda,
 (2020) 16 SCC 318] and in modification of the direction issued by the Commission, we direct
 that the interest on the refund shall be payable from the dates of deposit. Therefore, the
 appeal filed by purchaser deserves to be partly allowed. The interests shall be payable from
 the dates of such deposits.
33. At the same time, we are of the opinion that the interest of 9% granted by the
 Commission is fair and just and we find no reason to interfere in the appeal filed by the
 consumer for enhancement of interest.
3. On the other hand, Mr. Ramnik Gupta, on behalf of the respondent complainant
(Manjula Garg in FA/42/2022) has submitted that the rate of interest and the
cost-inclusive lump sum compensation of a small amount of about Rs. 1.35 lac for
mental agony suffered by the respondent allottee, as allowed by the State Commission,
 rather than being excessive, is on the lower side. In appeal no. FA/227/2023 filed by the
allottee, the appellant-allottee Asha Kumari assails the order of the State Commission
and prays for inter alia enhancing the rate of interest to 18-21% from that of 12%
granted by the State Commission.
3.1. Mr. Ramnik Gupta, counsel on behalf of the Respondent Ms. Manjula Garg has
contended that the grant of interest and the rate thereof as compensation after
rendering the finding of the deficiency in service of unreasonable delay in handing over
the possession as awarded by the State Commission is essentially a matter of
discretion to be exercised judiciously by the fora after taking into account the totality of
the facts and circumstances, and cannot necessarily be a matter of any precedent or
any alleged consistency with the observations or action of the Supreme Court rendered
in particular facts of the case decided by it. Majority of the decisions relied upon by the
appellant builder have been rendered in the context and background of the Covid-19
pandemic and rendered in the peculiar facts of those cases, when the building and
construction industry were under stress and the market had suffered a setback, which
allowed the frustrated allottees to get a new unit at relatively lower price if they so
desired, and, therefore also the same cannot be made basis for challenging the rate of
interest as granted on the facts of the present case by the State Commission after due
and judicious consideration. It has further been pointed out that in Rajnesh Sharma Vs.
M/s Business Park Town Planners Ltd. in Civil appeal no. 3998 of 2023, the Apex court,
in the facts of that case, has observed that the interest on refund granted at the rate of
9% by NCDRC will not serve the ends of justice and that the respondent builder cannot
be permitted to escape with a nominal liability. Therefore, the Supreme Court enhanced
the rate of interest from 9% to 18% by observing as under:
18. Having noted thus, we agree with Mr. Nayyar that before compensation can be
 granted by the NCDRC, actual loss must be proved to have been suffered by the
 consumer. The objective of granting compensation cannot be altered such that it amounts
 to a windfall gain to the other partay. Proof of actual loss would require evidence to be
 tendered, for, it is a guiding lamp for grant of compensation. Be that as it may, in this
 case, we are not deciding the actual loss suffered by the appellant. We are only
 concerned with deciding the rate of interest to be awarded to the appellant on the
 principal amount paid by him to the respondent.
19. Keeping in mind the overall conduct of the respondent: the delay caused by it in
 offering the plot, the fact that the respondent charged the appellant delay compensation
 @ 18% p.a. On the due amount, and the long wait that the appellant had to endure over
 a period of a decade, causing harassment and anxiety, which are writ large, we find that
 this is an appropriate case where refund of the principal amount with interest @ 9% p.a.,
 as awarded by the NDCRC, will not serve the ends of justice.
20. In view of the conduct of the respondent, it cannot be permitted to escape with a
 nominal liability for its default, while it charged interest @ 18% on default committed by
 the appellant. Although, the rate of interest charged by the builder cannot be granted to
 . the buyer as a rule of thumb,however, in the present case, equity and fairness demands
 that the respondent be put to the same rigors for charging 18% interest and face
 consequences similar to those imposed on the appellant for default committed by him. If
 we hold otherwise, we will be p perpetuating a manifestly wrong bargain.
21. We, therefore, substitute the rate of interest awarded by the NCDRC amd increase
 it from 9% to 18% per annum, while keeping the other terms intact. Respondent shall
 refund the requisite amount within a period of two months from date.
3.2. Similarly, reliance is placed on the following observations of the Supreme Court
in M/s Ashoka Investments Co. Vs. M/s United Towers India Pvt. Ltd. in C.A. No.
4913/2015 decided on 11.10.2022:
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and perusing the material on record, we
 enquired from the respondents, as to whether, the amount as awarded by the NCDRC in
 the impugned order dated 16.03.2015 has been paid to the appellant or not. We were
 informed that amount has not been paid so far. No pg. 5 justification has come forward as
 to why the awarded amount was not tendered to the appellant. The appellant has
 pressed for the entire complaint being allowed as per the relief claimed therein. On the
 other hand, the respondent has sought to justify the order of NCDRC. However, there is
 no appeal by the respondent. The appellant has also pressed vehemently that
 respondent should be called upon to produce the sale deeds of the two flats in question,
 transferred in favour of the third parties and that the said amount ought to be paid to the
 appellant along with other claims, the respondent has unjustly enriched itself by the
 aforesaid conduct. On the other hand, this request has been resisted by the respondents.
11. Having considered the submissions of the learned counsel for the parties, we are in
 agreement with the findings recorded by the NCDRC regarding the conduct of both the
 parties, however, we feel that in the fitness of things and in the interest of both the parties
 considering the nature of agreement made and also their conduct that the order of the
 NCDRC requires to be modified. The rate of interest awarded is only 9%. Once, we find
 that under the agreement, in the event of default, the appellant's liability to pay
 interest on the defaulted amount could go up to 18%, it would be just and proper in
 the facts of the present case that 18% interest be awarded on the refund amount.
12. We accordingly partly allow this appeal and in partial modification of the impugned
 order of the NCDRC, we direct that respondent will refund the amount of
 Rs.4,95,000/(four lakhs and ninetyfive thousand) being the total sale consideration to the
 appellant along with interest @ 18% per annum w.e.f. 17.01.1995 till the date, it is paid.
The said amount be paid at the earliest and in any case within a period of four weeks
 from today.
3.3 Drawing our attention to para 4 onwards, and para 14 in particular, of the State
Commission's order, on facts, it is stated by Mr. Gupta that the appellant has neither
pleaded nor brought any evidence on record even to explain or justify the delay in
handing over of the possession or to state the stage of completion of the project. The
appellant has been completely and adamantly unconcerned about the agony of the
allottees or its own obligation of timely completing the project and duly handing over the
possession and even in communicating the prospect or timelines for the same. It is
therefore, urged that the rate of interest, as granted by the State Commission after
 complete appreciation of the evidence on record and all relevant facts including the
conduct of the parties as discussed in the order, in the facts and circumstances, do not
require any interference. As such, if at all, in view of the fact that for delayed payments,
the builder as per the BBA was entitled to charge the interest at the rate of 21%, the
State Commission should ideally have awarded the interest at the rate of 21%.
4. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and perused the decisions
cited at the bar. There is no dispute that there is deficiency in service in as much as
handing over of the possession has been delayed beyond more than 3 1/2 years from
the agreed date of possession i.e. 36 months from the date of agreement. The only
grievance raised by the appellant builder in the present appeals in with regard to the
rate of interest and compensation for mental agony. The close perusal of the line of
judgments of the Supreme Court with regard to the rate of interest to be awarded in
cases of directions of refund of the consideration paid by the allottees, restricting such
interest rate to 9% relied upon by the appellant would indeed reveal that though it has
been opined therein that neither compensation under multiple heads can be granted nor
can the compensation granted can be excessive or unreasonable or disproportionate,
we are unable to find a binding mandate that under no circumstance can the interest to
be granted be more than 9% or that in all circumstances it has to be 9%. On the other
hand, in the Supreme Court recent decisions in Rajnesh Sharma and in Ashoka
Investments Co. Vs. M/s United Towers India Pvt. Ltd. in C.A. No. 4913/2015 decided
on 11.10.2022, it has been observed that there is no sacrosanct rule that interest
beyond 9% cannot be allowed in cases of directions for compensation by way of refund
due to deficient service by the developers. It has further been observed in these cases
that the overall circumstances would and should determine the compensatory rate of
interest. Following the same, we are of the considered opinion that all relevant factors
including the nature of deficiency, the length of the delay caused by the developer, the
reasons for such delay, the injury or loss, including the mental agony, suffered by the
complainant and even the prevalent market conditions and the current market price for
the complainant to get equivalent unit, and, the similar factors all should go into the
consideration of the fora while deciding the rate of interest to be allowed while directing
refund of the consideration paid by the complainant. Equally, the terms and condition in
the buyers agreement or in the allotment letter and the rate of interest stipulated therein
for delayed payment of instalment or for delay in handing over the possession would
also be a relevant consideration.
5. We note that in para 18, the State Commission has discussed the issue of rate of
interest with considerable detail and has duly and judiciously applied its mind to the
aspect of quantum of compensation through rate of interest. It is the categorical
observation of the State Commission that compensation cannot be uniform, which
observation resonates fully with the observations of the Supreme Court in Rajnesh
Sharma. It has been further noted by the State Commission that in cases of directions
for refund of the amounts, the allottee suffers the loss of escalation of the price of that
unit and he would need to take out more money from his pocket for beating the
escalation in price and therefore after referring to a number of decisions of Supreme
Court and of this Commission, has come to a considered and judicious conclusion that
the award of interest at 12% per annum would serve the ends of justice. The
respondent appears right in contending that the similar unit cannot now, in the present
rising market scenario, be purchased by him even with the compensation as awarded .
by the State Commission. We also note that the builder, for delayed payment of
instalments by the allottees, has stipulated charging of interest at 18/21%, though that
factor being relevant, that alone cannot be the measure for awarding compensatory
interest. In the present appeal while heavy reliance has been placed by the appellant
on Supreme Court decisions awarding interest at 9% in cases of refund, the appellant
builder has also relied on Clause 5.3 (c) to contend that the pre-agreed rate of interest
in cases of failure of the developer to offer the plots is 9% and therefore, no more than
9% could have been awarded by the State Commission on that count also. We in this
behalf, however, note that Clause 5.1 (c) provides for suo motu and proactive action of
tendering refund by the developer. The same criteria obviously cannot and should not
apply when the allottee has suffered due to deficient service and has earned the
entitlement to such rightful refund after a strenuous wait of nearly five years and after a
legal battle of nearly two years. Apart from stating the rate of interest as granted by the
State Commission to be excessive, the appellant has not been able to point out
objectively any error in the finding of the State Commission or the logic of
proportionality qua the rate of interest as adopted by the State Commission. No case
has been made out to the effect that the actual injury or financial loss suffered by the
complainants on account of the non-delivery of the units within the stipulated time is
less than the compensation granted by way of interest as granted. We are of the
considered opinion that the quantum of compensation, when challenged in the appeal,
the interference by us can be only when the same is on the ground and basis of the
 compensation being demonstrably either gross and apparently excessive or low, or
palpably disproportionate, or apparently arbitrary, or being wholly based on no
 s

evidence, and has also to be based and established to be so on facts and evidence
relating to quantum of injury or loss suffered. As such, no such effort or such ground
has been made out by the appellant for us to interfere with the judicial discretion
exercised reasonably and judiciously by the State Commission in arriving at and
granting quantum of compensation through the rate of interest of 12% as granted. We
also find no error in the direction of the State Commission with regard to the penal
interest of 3% per annum in case of default by the OP in making the payment before
the due date. Though the lumpsum award of Rs. 1.35 lacs towards "mental agony and
costs" opens a new and second head of compensation, after noting that the amount
granted is composite inclusive of the costs, and after noting the smallness of the
amount of award under this head, we, in appellate jurisdiction, decline to interfere. We,
thus finding no valid reason to interfere, fully uphold the order of the State Commission.
In the result, the appeals FA/42/2022, FA/43/2022 and FA/44/2022 filed by the OP
builder are dismissed.
6. The appeal FA/227/2023 has been filed by Asha Kumari with reported delay of
402 days. On the day of the hearing, nobody was present to press the appeal. The
delay condonation application being IA/2295/2023 has been filed wherein the reasons
for delay are stated to be financial constraints of the complainant who is a retired
school teacher, inability to pay the counsel fees and the medical expenses which
became necessary in the year 2017 and 2019. After considering the specific reasons
as detailed in the application, and the reply of the respondent received on 14.01.2025
vide diary no. 1480, we, in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, deem it
proper to condone the delay. Turning to the merits, however, we note that the State
Commission has already granted refund along with interest at 12%. The appellant is
seeking enhancement in the rate of interest. The appellant has relied on the fact that
the Buyers agreement para 2.4 allowed the rate of interest of 18-21% for delayed
payment of instalments by the allottees and therefore, the interest granted by the State
Commission is erroneously on the lower side. The appellant also relied on various
decisions of this Commission and the Supreme Court wherein interest at the rate of
18% or higher has been granted. The appellant also pleaded that a loan of Rs.15 lakhs
from the HDFC bank was taken for obtaining the said property on which substantial
interest had been paid without any corresponding benefit of acquiring the property and
 e

 therefore also the rate of interest to be awarded by the State Commission needed to be
 in the range of 18 to 21%. Having considered the contentions and having perused the
 file, and for the reasons as already discussed, we are unable to find any convincing
 reason or basis to interfere with the well-reasoned order of the State Commission and
 with the well-founded basis for award of compensation as adopted by the State
 Commission. We, therefore, find no merit in the appeal and the same is dismissed.
7. In the result, all the four appeals are dismissed.
